facts.statement: Perugyps lived during the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene epochs.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Miocene - Early Pliocene ~

facts.statement: The genus Perugyps was described by Stucchi and Emslie in 2005.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Stucchi & Emslie, 2005

facts.statement: Perugyps was described based on isolated fossil remains including wing parts, leg bones, and a lower jaw.
facts.quote: It was described in 2005 on the basis of a number of isolated fossil remains including various parts of the wings, the legs and even a lower jaw.

facts.statement: Perugyps was found in the Pisco Formation of Peru.
facts.quote: Perugyps is an extinct genus of condor from the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene Pisco Formation of Peru

facts.statement: Fossil evidence suggests Perugyps was approximately 7% larger than the Andean condor.
facts.quote: The fossil remains suggest that Perugyps was a large bird, perhaps around 7% larger than the Andean condor

facts.statement: Researchers speculate that Perugyps fed on marine mammal carcasses similar to modern vultures.
facts.quote: It has been speculated that Perugyps would have fed on the carcasses of the numerous marine mammals of the Pisco Formation like modern vultures

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that Perugyps also snatched chicks from local seabird colonies to supplement its diet.
facts.quote: and that it could have also added to its diet by snatching chicks from the local seabird colonies.

facts.statement: The fossils were discovered at the Montemar and Sacaco Sur localities in Peru's Pisco Formation.
facts.quote: Perugyps was described in 2005 by Marcelo Stucchi and Steven D. Emslie following the discovery of several isolated fossil bones at the Montemar (6.0–4.5 Ma) and Sacaco Sur localities of Peru's Pisco Formation.

facts.statement: The name Perugyps combines the country of origin, Peru, with the Greek word for vulture.
facts.quote: The name Perugyps is derived from the animals country of origin, Peru, in combination with the Greek word "gyps" meaning "vulture".

facts.statement: The species name diazi honors Eusebio Díaz.
facts.quote: The species was named in honor of Eusebio Díaz.

facts.statement: Specific features of the carpometacarpus identify Perugyps as a condor.
facts.quote: In the type description, Stucchi and Emslie note that the carpometacarpus of Perugyps preserves several features identifying it as a condor.

facts.statement: The anterior carpal fossa of Perugyps is less pneumatic than in modern birds.
facts.quote: The anterior carpal fossa is described as less pneumatic than in extant forms.

facts.statement: The proximal symphysis of the Perugyps carpometacarpus is short, similar to the Andean condor.
facts.quote: The fused section at the base of the bone, the proximal symphysis, is short like in the Andean condor

facts.statement: The coronoid process of the Perugyps lower jaw is taller than in any living vulture.
facts.quote: The coronoid process of the dentary is taller than in any living cathartiid.

facts.statement: The total length of the Perugyps lower jaw exceeds that of both modern condor species.
facts.quote: In total dimensions the lower jaw of Perugyps was longer than those of both modern condor species.

facts.statement: The area between the condyles on the Perugyps tarsometatarsus is deeper than in all living vultures and the extinct Geronogyps.
facts.quote: The area between the condyles is deeper than in all living cathartiids and even Geronogyps

facts.statement: Perugyps is distinguished by a distal external trochlea placed lower than the middle trochlea, unlike extant cathartids.
facts.quote: The bone is diagnosed by possessing a distal external trochlea that is placed as low or even lower than the middle trochlea, which sets it apart from extant cathartiids in which it is placed higher up.

facts.statement: Degrange and colleagues estimate Perugyps was about 7% larger than the modern Andean condor and Vultur messii.
facts.quote: According to Degrange and colleagues Perugyps was approximately 7% larger than modern Andean condors and the extinct Vultur messii

facts.statement: Stucchi and Emslie classified Perugyps as a condor based on three distinct characters of the carpometacarpus.
facts.quote: Perugyps was first classified as a condor by Stucchi and Emslie in their 2005 description based on what they describe as three clear characters of the carpometacarpus

facts.statement: A 2015 study suggests Perugyps is closely associated with other South American condors like Gymnogyps howardae, Geronogyps, and the Andean condor.
facts.quote: In the 2015 description of Kuntur Stucchi and colleagues find a closer association between that taxon and other South American condors including Gymnogyps howardae, Geronogyps, the Andean condor and Perugyps.

facts.statement: Perugyps fossils were found in the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene Pisco Formation at the Montemar and Sacaco Sur localities.
facts.quote: Perugyps has been recovered from two localities of the Late Miocene to Early Pliocene Pisco Formation, specifically the localities of Montemar and Sacaco Sur.

facts.statement: The localities where Perugyps was found represent ancient coastal environments with protected beaches and reefs.
facts.quote: in the case of Montemar and Sacaco Sur specifically environments consisting of protected beaches and reefs exposed to the currents.

facts.statement: Perugyps likely fed primarily on the diverse seabirds and marine mammals that shared its coastal habitat.
facts.quote: This diverse fauna of both seabirds and marine mammals was likely the backbone of Perugyps′ diet.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Perugyps acted as a scavenger of marine mammal carcasses and may have also preyed on live bird chicks.
facts.quote: Stucchi and Emslie suggest that much like Andean condors living along the Peruvian coast today it could have fed on the carcasses of marine mammals and may have even snatched the chicks of other birds while still alive.

facts.statement: The species was named by M. Stucchi and S. D. Emslie in 2005.
facts.quote: Fue nombrado por M. Stucchi y S. D. Emslie, 2005.

facts.statement: The genus Perugyps was established by M. Stucchi and S. D. Emslie in 2005.
facts.quote: genus_authority: M. Stucchi y S. D. Emslie, 2005

facts.statement: Perugyps is classified within the family Cathartidae.
facts.quote: familia: Cathartidae

facts.statement: The order of Perugyps is uncertain, with its family placed in Falconiformes, Accipitriformes, Ciconiiformes, or Cathartiformes.
facts.quote: ordo: Incertae sedis (Se ubica a la familia en Falconiformes, Accipitriformes, Ciconiiformes o Cathartiformes)

facts.statement: Perugyps belongs to the subfamily Vulturinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Vulturinae

facts.statement: Perugyps lived between 7.246 and 5.333 million years ago during the Messinian age.
facts.quote: Time range: Messinian to Messinian (7.246 to 5.333 million years ago)

facts.statement: Perugyps diazi was found in the Pisco Formation in the Ica department of Peru.
facts.quote: P. diazi fue encontrado en la formación Pisco, en el departamento de Ica, Perú.

facts.statement: Perugyps diazi was a scavenger that lived on the beaches of modern-day Pisco alongside a high biodiversity of marine birds, whales, sharks, and giant penguins.
facts.quote: Era un carroñero que vivía en las playas de la actual Pisco, junto con una gran biodiversidad de aves marinas, ballenas, tiburones, pingüinos gigantes, etc.

rejected.statement: The holotype, a partial carpometacarpus, was collected by Marcelo Stucchi in 2000.
rejected.quote: The holotype, a partial carpometacarpus, was collected by Stucchi personally in 2000
